triggers.text: The great door. Ninety years of paint and nobody has ever seen it open.
No ceiling. The light is white and comes from everywhere, and the ground goes on until it stops being ground.
Wheel ruts, old but used. Somebody comes this way — not often.
Shale. Mud-brick and scrap around two pumps, a saloon, a flag that was a sheet once. Twenty-odd houses and a lot of empty ones.
Shale. Mud-brick and scrap around two pumps, a saloon, a flag that was a sheet once. Twenty-odd houses and a lot of empty ones.
The pumps run in short bursts, then stop, then run — on a clock nobody in Shale set.

barks: Race you to the pumps!
Mam says the Dogs eat kids.
Did you see the kite?
Mags waters it. Everyone knows.
One more and then home.

triggers.text: The dead highway lies across the sky on its piers, and under it, in the shade, the Rust Dogs have made a town out of what the highway dropped.
Shale's water, in a tank with Shale's name still stencilled on it.

barks: Looking or buying?
Posted prices.
Race you to the well!
Mam says don't.
Did you see the kite?

triggers.text: Tollhouse 9. A wall of poured concrete across the old highway, a tower with a lamp, and a gate with two sets of sandbags. Everything east of here is somebody's.
Tollhouse 9, from the inside. The wall looks the same from both sides, which is the point.
The highway runs on east. The guard at the far posts looks for a stamp you do not have.
The outriders' yard: two bikes with the guild's half-moon on the tank, a rifle scabbard on one, and the smell of fuel nobody else in the Sallow can buy.
A cage of chain-link inside the warehouse, with a cot in it and a chalk tally on the wall: days, and a sum going down very slowly.

barks: Guild water's dear.
Waiting on the caravan.
Don't look at the cage.

triggers.text: Signal Hill. A mast on the skyline with a red light that still blinks, slow as a pulse, and a track that goes up to it in switchbacks cut by somebody who meant them to last.
The top of Signal Hill. The Sallow lies under you like a map of itself: the highway, the salt pans, a line of dead windpumps to the south-east, and far west a grey smear that is Shale.
Dry Wells. Three wells with nothing in them, a water tower with something in it, and a pump station that was built to outlast the town and has.
The pump hall. Two pumps the size of houses, hammering on and off on a clock nobody in this building set, and a line going north under the floor to Shale.
The control room: a console, a pressure panel, and a chair that has not been sat in since the Burn. Something green is still lit.

The windpump graveyard. Six towers in a line across the pan, vanes locked, pumping nothing, and under them stone troughs with the dark stain of water that is not there any more. Something small bolts from the nearest trough as you come up.

The troughs are dry, but the sand around them is written over with tracks: hare, something with hooves, something with claws that walks on two toes. Game still comes here out of habit, at dawn and dusk.
Cart ruts, many and deep, going east off the pan toward a long low hill. Horse dung, not old. Something with a lot of wheels camps that way.

The pan. White to the edge of the world, and in the middle of it, where nothing should be, a truck on its side with its load spilled, and a dark scar in the crust behind it half a mile long. Nothing moves. The glare makes your eyes water.
A ring pressed into the crust, forty feet across, the salt fused glassy at the rim. Something heavy sat here. In the middle of it, something smaller still does.

The burnt orchard. Rows of black trees the Burn left standing, and among them a dozen with leaves on, which is a thing you have not seen in your life: green, in rows, with people kneeling at their feet.

barks: Mam says the horses first.
Race you to the water wagon!
Are you from a town? What's a town like?

triggers.text: Ninebridge. The old highway walks out over a gorge on nine concrete legs and a town has grown on its back: tents and stalls and welded boxes the whole length of the deck, lamps on poles, a hum of people buying. The ninth span is missing. Below, a river that has not run in ninety years.
Ninebridge, from the east: the road runs down to a gorge and a bridge with a town on it, and the first thing on this bank is a metal platform with a cage.
The deck ends in air. The ninth span lies in the riverbed in three pieces, with a market stall still bolted to one of them. The way across is four planks along the south parapet.
The auction block: a welded platform, a counter, and a cage with a cot in it. A chalk board lists today's lots by number and sum. The sums are people.
The porters' camp under the west ramp: tents, a fire, and forty people who carry the bridge's goods on their backs when the guild says carry — sitting down, today, with their straps off.

barks: Paper's up again.
Twelve for the crossing, and they call it a bridge.
Don't buy futures from a man who smiles.
The ninth span? Fell the year the river stopped.
Straps off. Straps stay off.
They forecast we lose. Let them carry it, then.
Three days, they said. We can sit three days.
Lot four's young. That'll go high.
I came for a cook. They've only got debtors.
Fen hates it. He's good at it, though.
Mind the planks.
Guild deck. Guild rules.

of_shrine_sign.name: The sign of the open sky

triggers.text: Openfield. Rows and rows of green in the glass, which is a thing you have seen once before in your life, on a smaller scale, north of Shale; two long timber halls; a well with a wheel on it; and people in grey scarves bending to the soil who straighten as you come, and look at the sky, and go back to it.
Openfield, from the east: a burial ground of cairns under a dead windpump, and past it the green rows the Choir has coaxed out of the glass.
The fields. Every third row is grey: leaves curled and spotted, stalks gone soft at the root, the smell of something sweet going wrong. The rows between are green and do not know yet.
The burial ground: cairns in rows under the open sky, no names on them, a dead windpump turning for nobody. One grave is new.

barks: Every third row. We pull it and it comes back.
The sky keeps no books.
Don't drink from the north trough; the Elder says.
Sing or don't. The soil doesn't mind.
Are you from the bridge? Did you see the planks?
Petra says don't talk to strangers. You're a stranger.
I can sing the whole sky-song. All of it.
They feed us first. First! Nobody ever fed us first.
Came from the Sump. Don't go to the Sump.

triggers.text: The Sump. A concrete bowl sunk in the glass where the city's storm drains once came up for air, pumped dry by hand and picked over by two camps that do not speak: scrap cabins on the west rim, tents on the east, and between them, at the bowl's north end, a tunnel mouth with sandbags across it and a lamp burning in daylight.
The bowl: wrecks, drums, a crane-arm somebody has been trying to raise for a year, and a machine on its side with its legs folded, the city's kind, dead so long the scavengers use it as a bench.

barks: Grel says the tunnel's ours. The Tanners say otherwise. The guild says keep digging.
Scrip on the fourth day. Always the fourth day.
Don't cross the bowl after dark.
Hesk says the tunnel's ours. Grel says otherwise. The guild pays both, which should tell you something.
There's a door down there that never opened.
West rim's got the better cabins. We've got the better knives.

triggers.text: The tunnel comes up through a hole the Sump cut in a pump-room floor. Pumps like Cistern 9's. A supply pipe like Cistern 9's, cut through, dry. The lamp the scavengers hung still burns. Everything else has been dark for forty years, and smells of it.
A line on the corridor wall at shoulder height, brown, where water stood for a season after the pumps stopped and then went down and did not come back.
The dormitory. The cots are made. Some of them are not empty, and have not been for forty years, and lie the way people lie who decided to.
The great-door hall. Sandbags against the inside of the door, and crates, and a table, and then — the marks are still on the floor — the sandbags dragged away again, and the door still shut.

exits.label: The stair down to the Sink
The avenue east, to Old Market

triggers.text: Meridian. Towers first, miles off, grey against grey; then the Wall, poured concrete five storeys high, running out of sight both ways; then, when the road reaches it, a gate the size of a door, a booth, a lamp, and a line of people who have been waiting since before you came over the last rise.

The Precinct. Swept asphalt, lamps that all work, a tram rail, buildings with numbers on them, and people walking as if they had somewhere to be by a time. Nobody looks at you. A camera on the lamp-post does.
A square between the tenements with a standpipe, a bell on a post, and a notice board under glass. Everything that happens here has been posted first.
The Loop's Precinct platform: a raised deck, a shelter, a tram on the rail with its doors open and nobody in it, and a board of district names with a fare beside each.

barks: Curfew's at nine. The bell's never late.
Mind the camera; it minds you.
Water's rationed since the Sallow business. Point eight.
The schedule holds.
Papers.
Keep to the avenue after dark.
Third day in the line. They say the hearing's Tuesday.
The Ring's burning again. They don't care.
My face isn't on their machine. That's the whole problem.

exits.label: The avenue west, to the Precinct
The stair down to the Sink
The east street, to Lantern Row

triggers.text: Old Market. The avenue gives out at a dead mall with its roof gone and a thousand people inside it, and the streets round it are stalls, and the stalls are everything: noodles, cells, cartridges, cloth, paper, chrome in boxes, a tram that still runs and a kiosk that still talks. Nobody here walks as if they had somewhere to be by a time.

The mall's central court under the open sky: a dead escalator, a metal deck worn bright, pink and blue light from tubes somebody salvaged, and a container with a hatch in it and a board beside the hatch, which is where everyone in Meridian who needs something done ends up looking.

The standpipe square. The dial is turned down and the queue is forty long and getting louder, and the two wardens at the square's edge have the look of men counting. Somebody at the front says the Precinct drinks what the market doesn't.
The east street runs on toward Lantern Row under strings of dead bulbs and a warden who says WORKS before you ask.

barks: Half-Price pays half. That's the name.
Don't buy chrome from a box you can't open.
The kiosk said my name. It said my dead name.
The Precinct drinks what we don't.
Wardens count the market twice a day and never like the answer.
Point eight. For us it's point six.
The dial's theirs. The thirst's ours.
Auntie Wen's. Two Tolls, a bowl. Three, with meat; don't ask which.
Best gossip in Meridian is in this queue.

exits.label: The stair up to the Precinct
The stair up to Old Market

triggers.text: The Sink. The stair comes down out of the Precinct's lamplight into a dark that drips, and the dark is a city: the old streets under the elevated road, flooded to the knee, flooded to the roof, lit by work-lamps on cables and by nothing. Boardwalks on stilts go out across the water to where people live. Something is pumping, far off, slowly, like a heart that has been told to.

The Sink, by the market stair: a concrete shelf, a kettle, a wall of names, and below it the dark water of the under-city with its boardwalks going out across it on stilts. Something is pumping, far off, slowly.

The first pier of the stilt-walk has lines chalked up its side, one above the other, each with a year. The top line is above your head. Somebody has chalked next spring's already, a hand higher, with a question mark.
The pump house: the one building in the Sink with the Precinct's white lamps on it, and two wardens at its door who are not here to keep the Sink dry. Through the wall, the slow thud of the pumps.
The clinic: a brick shell with a sodium lamp over the door and a queue that has learned to sit. The only light in the Sink that is the colour of a kitchen.
Three people with no chrome and skin the colour of the water stand up from a fire as you come along the walk. Nobody says anything. It is the kind of nobody that means turn round.

barks: Line's a hand higher this year.
Pumps run for the Precinct. We run for the stairs.
Ocho's free. Ocho's always free. Don't ask what it costs him.
Don't go east on the walk. The Pale don't like faces.
Sit. The queue sits.
Vash buys. Vash buys anything that was ever warm.
Spring's coming up the stair this year, you watch.
Mind the third board.
Water's warm. That's the worst of it.

exits.label: The street west, to Old Market

triggers.text: Lantern Row. The street comes out of Old Market's dead bulbs into live ones: salvaged tubes in every colour that still lights, strung over a canal that throws them back. Music from three doors at once, none of it the same song. A bridge, a boat, a queue outside something pink. Somebody is shouting odds.
The Loop's Lantern Row stop: a metal deck with a tram on it and the Row going away south under its tubes, pink and cyan and gold, over the black line of the canal. Somebody is shouting odds.

The pit: a sunk metal floor inside a chain fence, four white lamps, bleachers of crates, and a card on a post with tonight's names. The crowd stands three deep. The floor has been washed and it shows.
The Lantern: a container with a violet tube over the door and a smell of warm electronics. Reveries by the hour. The sign says MEMORIES — YOURS OR BETTER.
The street runs on east under dead tubes toward Bridgeward, and a chain across it with a sign: WORKS. Two Gilt lean on the chain and do not say works.

barks: Anvil's three to one. He's always three to one.
The Velvet's a queue tonight. Try the hall.
Don't buy a reverie you can't put down.
Gilt pay in Crown coin. Don't take it; it's counted.
Somebody's stranger on the card again.
Twenty on the small one.
He went down in the second last week. Took the dive, you watch.
Mab pays. Mab always pays. That's why Mab's rich.
Boat's two. Bridge is free and further.
Canal's warm. Don't ask.

triggers.text: The Stacks. Two megablocks a street apart and forty floors high, grey, each window a different light, each balcony a different washing. The street between them is a canyon with a tram at the bottom of it. Somewhere above you a thousand doors are shutting for the night.

Block Seven's lobby: a concrete hall the height of three floors with a market in it, a board of floor notices, a committee office with a door, and a stairwell in a cage. The lifts are dead; there is a panel beside them that says so in the Plan's own words.

barks: Nine's dry again. Twelve's pumping.
Forty floors and the lift says *as per schedule*.
Committee meets in the lobby. Everyone shouts; Hester writes.
Don't rent above twenty. The water doesn't.
Fitch has water. Fitch always has water; ask him whose.
The board says Nine, Twelve and the roof. The board always says that.
Stairs. Nine floors. I count them every night.

exits.label: Down: nine floors to the lobby

triggers.text: Floor nine. A corridor of doors round a dead core, lit by lamps on cables that somebody keeps lit; washing on lines between the lamps; the smell of a hundred stoves. Every door has a number and most have a name chalked under it. 9-14 has neither.

barks: Nine's dry. Twelve's pumping. Same every night.
Hester says the committee's meeting. Hester's been saying.
Ulla hears the lifts. Ulla hears everything that's stopped.
9-14's been empty since the Marrs went to the Ring.

triggers.text: The roof of Block Seven, forty floors up: the whole of Meridian under you in its haze, the Spire a grey needle to the south, the Wall a line, the Sallow beyond it going to nothing. Up here the air moves. A tank on a pad in the middle; beds of real dirt to the west with things growing in them; a deck of trays to the east under an awning, greener, humming. Two groups of people who are not looking at each other.

barks: Beds are dry by noon. Tank's full by six. Do the sum.
Twelve pumps at two. I hear it through the floor.
Mama Deel grew tomatoes up here the year I was born.
Trays don't need dirt. Trays need the tank.
Latch comes Thursdays. Don't talk to Latch.
Best view in Meridian and nobody comes up for it.
You can see the Sink from here if you know where it isn't.

exits.label: The chain west, to Lantern Row

triggers.text: Bridgeward. The chain behind you, and ahead a street of chop-shops and salvage heaps running to a bridge that goes out over nothing and stops. Three kinds of paint on the walls, each over the other. A red light blinks on a mast. Somebody at the bridgehead is charging money to stand on it.
The Loop's Bridgeward stop, a metal deck over a street of salvage with a broken bridge at the end of it and a red light blinking on a mast. Three kinds of paint on every wall.

The bridgehead: a chain across the deck, a booth, two Rustmouths with shotguns and a slate of prices, and beyond them the bridge going out over the dry river to where it isn't any more. A notice on the booth in Crown print.

The Saints' tower: a dead relay mast with a red lamp on it that somebody keeps lit, and under it a brick shell full of radios that do not work, arranged like an altar, and people sitting with them, listening.
The deck ends in torn rebar and air. Forty feet down, the dry river; across it, the far bank and the Docks' cranes, close enough to hear and no way to reach.

barks: Toll's five to stand on a bridge that goes nowhere.
Three paints on the wall. Mine's under all of them.
The girl at the tower said my name yesterday. I've never met her.
Rustmouths take for the Crown. Gilt take for the Gilt. Pale take what you've got two of.
The Dogs had the garage. Then the Rustmouths had the bridge. Then the Dogs had the Sallow.
Haul's weighed Fridays.
Boss says the Crown pays by the car. The Crown doesn't know what a car is.
Listen. There — under the hiss.
She says true things. That's the trouble with her.

triggers.text: The Crown's lift lobby. The car that costs nothing opens on tile that has been washed, a lens on a post with a green light under it, and two wardens whose grey is clean. Through the gate, light: real light, through glass, on leaves. Nobody here is in a hurry, which is the first thing money buys.

The terraces. Domes of old glass over a promenade of planters that are green all the way through, a pool that reflects a sky it does not have to share, and a hall at the end with its doors open on music. The air has no taste at all. People in clothes that have never been mended look at you the way the lens did, and decide, and go on.
Through the gate over three wardens. Somewhere a bell has started that is not for dinner, and the people on the promenade are going indoors the way birds go off a field.

decision.text: You went into the Crown over its wardens.

news.text: somebody went up to the Crown over the lift wardens during the Masque

triggers.text: The Masque. A hall under the biggest dome, lit like noon at night, strings somewhere, and a hundred people in the Crown's season showing their faces to one another and to the lens over the door, which is the point of a Masque up here: everyone is seen. At the far end a lectern with the Committee's crest, and nobody at it yet.

A studio: a chair in good light, a machine that hums, and the walls hung with portraits of people who look like the people on the promenade but better, older, finished. Under each a date that has not happened yet.
House Ashby-Crane's salon: older money than the hall, quieter, a crest over the door with a crane on it, and a girl at the window who is not looking at the view.
The kitchens: heat, steam, forty people in white moving fast, and a lift that goes down to Old Market with the day's rubbish and the night's help. Nobody up here has ever seen this room.

The parapet. Under it, all of Meridian in haze: the Precinct a grid, Old Market a stain, the canal a thread, the Stacks a wall, the broken bridge a finger pointing at the Docks. You cannot see the Sink at all. That is the point of up here.

barks: Vane's season. Everyone says so, so it must be.
The near end. Have you heard? The near end of a bridge.
The Concern sent a man. The Concern never sends a man.
I don't go down. Fenwick goes down. Look what it did to him.
The Chair, tonight. They say the file already knows.
Honora won't duel. Honora buys.
Smile. The lens likes a smile.
Forty covers. Forty! For people who don't eat.
Down by the lift at four, or walk.
Don't look at them. They don't look at you.
Green all the way through. It's the water. They have the water.
Mind the beds.
